statement: Across New York City's UHF42 neighbourhoods, a higher share of workers who walk or cycle to work goes with a lower share of adults with obesity, after adjusting for neighbourhood poverty.

graph_evidence.summary: 21 ratio findings; 11 above 1, 10 below; 6 with CI above 1, 7 with CI below 1; median ratio 1.2 (mixed increments and designs)
3 ratio findings; 2 above 1, 1 below; 2 with CI above 1, 1 with CI below 1; median ratio 1.96 (mixed increments and designs)

graph_evidence.note: The graph's physical activity -> obesity findings are split in sign (the ratio findings mix 'activity predicts lower obesity' with 'inactivity predicts higher obesity', so the sign of a ratio depends on the coding of the exposure). There is no concept for cycling or active commuting; variable search finds a few commuting variables (e.g. 'active commuting to/from school', 'being a non-active commuter').

literature.citation: Flint E, Cummins S, Sacker A (2014). Associations between active commuting, body fat, and body mass index: population based, cross sectional study in the United Kingdom. BMJ 349:g4887.
literature.finding: Men commuting by active or public modes had BMI about 1 kg/m2 lower than car commuters; women about 0.7 kg/m2.

literature.citation: Celis-Morales CA et al. (2017). Association between active commuting and incident cardiovascular disease, cancer, and mortality. BMJ 357:j1456.
literature.finding: Cycle commuting associated with lower CVD incidence and mortality (UK Biobank).

prediction.magnitude: Unadjusted slope: -2 to -6 percentage points of adult obesity per 10 points of walk-or-bike commute share. Poverty-adjusted: -0.5 to -4 points per 10 points.
prediction.support_if: Poverty-adjusted slope below 0 with a 95% interval below 0.
prediction.refute_if: Poverty-adjusted slope at or above 0 with an interval that excludes -0.5.

plan: Data: EHDP (github.com/nychealth/EHDP-data, commit 547482b9df589006543e13e8cdf6546e00ed9998): indicator 2415 commuting modes, measures 1304 (bicycle %) + 1307 (walked %), UHF42, ACS 2015-19; indicator 2063 adult obesity %, measure 506, UHF42, mean of 2017, 2018 and 2019 (CHS, self-reported BMI); indicator 103 poverty %, measure 221, UHF42, 2015-19. Model: OLS of obesity % on active-commute % (per 10 points), then adding poverty %; HC3 standard errors; sensitivity adding borough fixed effects and excluding Manhattan. Figure: scatter of UHF neighbourhoods coloured by poverty with the fitted adjusted slope and the slope implied by Flint et al. (about -1 kg/m2 BMI for active commuters, translated to obesity prevalence only qualitatively).
alternatives: Income, education and race/ethnicity composition (poverty is the named confounder; others are not measured here)
Density and Manhattan: walking to work is common where jobs are close, which is also where incomes are high
Reverse causation and selection: people with lower BMI choose to walk or cycle, or choose walkable neighbourhoods
Commute mode covers workers only; obesity covers all adults
registrant: mobility agent (Claude Opus 5.5), for J. Vernon
